lead.headline: Apple Puts the II in a Carrying Case
lead.dek: The $1,295 Apple IIc brings 128K, a built-in disk drive and nearly a decade of Apple II software into a compact 7.5-pound package.
body: SAN FRANCISCO — Apple Computer unveiled the Apple IIc on April 24 at its “Apple II Forever” dealer convention, putting the durable Apple II design into an ivory case small enough to carry by its handle. Even a 6.2-magnitude earthquake shaking Moscone Center could not upstage the week’s landmark personal-computer announcement.

At $1,295, the IIc includes a 1.02 MHz 65C02 processor, 128K of memory, Applesoft BASIC, a full-stroke keyboard and a built-in 5.25-inch floppy drive. The 7.5-pound machine is compact rather than truly cordless, but a broad set of ports accommodates a display, printer, modem, mouse or joystick and a second disk drive.

Compatibility is the strongest card in Apple’s hand. The company says roughly 90 percent of some 10,000 Apple II programs will run on the newcomer, letting families, schools and small offices keep their established software. Period reports say dealers placed more than 50,000 orders within hours.

The IIc also introduces Frog Design’s clean “Snow White” styling and extends Macintosh ideas to the older family through a $99 mouse bundled with MousePaint. Accessories range from a $199 green-screen monitor and $299 Scribe printer to a planned $600 flat display.

Apple is signaling that Macintosh and Apple II will advance together: one experiments with a graphical future, while the other carries a vast installed base into a friendlier shell. The IIc is evolutionary inside, but its combination of polish, portability and software breadth makes this an extra-edition week.

stories.headline: Apple II Forever, Apple III No More
body: Apple used the IIc debut to reassure dealers that Macintosh would not displace its established eight-bit line. The “Apple II Forever” theme turned compatibility and continuity into the convention’s rallying cry.

The same day brought the end of the troubled Apple III, Apple’s unsuccessful attempt to build a business successor to the II. The company now presents two clearer families: the profitable Apple II line for homes and schools, and Macintosh for its new graphical ambitions.
COMPUTE! later reported nearly two million Apple II-family machines sold, while Macintosh passed 70,000 in its first 100 days. Apple is pruning a failure while doubling down on its strongest names.

stories.headline: IBM’s PCjr Stumbles Out of the Gate
body: Reports immediately before this week say IBM’s PCjr is selling below expectations, sharpening the contest between two similarly priced family computers. Both the 128K PCjr and IIc offer a floppy drive, external power supply and ties to a larger software family.

Creative Computing finds the IIc keyboard markedly better, while noting the PCjr’s faster processor, side-bus expansion and cartridge slots. IBM’s machine retains the gravitational pull of the PC name, but its compromised keyboard and compatibility questions are proving costly.
Apple’s new entry makes ease of use and a proven library the center of the pitch. The home-computer contest will turn on what buyers can actually do after opening the box.

stories.headline: Software Becomes the Machine’s Magic
body: TIME’s April software cover calls programs “the magic carpet to the future,” capturing an industry shift from hardware novelty toward applications and usability. Apple’s IIc pitch makes the same argument through compatibility rather than raw processor power.
AppleWorks combines word processing, a database and a spreadsheet for the Apple II family. MousePaint, bundled with the IIc mouse, brings a Macintosh-style pointing interface to the older line.
The machine matters, but the library increasingly closes the sale. In 1984, useful programs—and the confidence that they will keep running—are becoming the most persuasive specification.

stories.headline: April’s Game Shelf Spans Machines
body: Computer Entertainer’s April issue finds a lively home-game shelf despite the console trade’s contraction. B.C.’s Quest for Tires and Fathom appear for Apple II, Oil’s Well for ColecoVision and Dragonhawk for Commodore 64.

Publishers continue to cross incompatible formats, searching for players on every popular machine. Arcade conversions share shelf space with original computer games, while reviews and mail-order listings help buyers navigate the crowded field.

Exact release days are often elusive, so these are April shelf sightings rather than claims of launch-day precision. They nevertheless show software variety remaining one of home computing’s strongest attractions.
